name: Cervical traction

lead: Cervical traction applies a gentle pulling force to the neck, in a clinic or with a home device. Posture-focused users try it hoping to ease a forward head position and improve neck curve and profile.

The chain is the neck gently stretched, neck tension eased, then the head carried further back. Physical therapists use it mainly for neck pain with nerve-root symptoms such as cervical radiculopathy. Guideline evidence is described as low quality, and some reviews report short-term pain relief when traction is added to physiotherapy. No study of appearance was found.

paras: Sessions are done with clinic equipment or home over-door and inflatable devices, usually for short periods repeated over weeks. In physio it is typically combined with exercise.
The reviewed sources do not detail risks. Neck symptoms can have other causes, so people with persistent pain, numbness or weakness may want to see a clinician before using it.

angle.text: Posture-focused users try cervical traction to ease a forward head position and improve neck curve and profile. The path runs from a gentle neck stretch to eased tension to the head carried further back. Physiotherapists use it for nerve-root neck pain; its effect on posture appearance has not been tested.

lead: Cervical traction applies a gentle pulling force to the neck, by hand in a clinic or with a mechanical or home device, to open space between vertebrae and ease pressure on neck structures. Physical therapists use it mainly for neck pain with nerve-root symptoms (cervical radiculopathy), often alongside exercise and manual therapy.[1][2][3]

In looksmaxxing and posture circles, neck traction devices are discussed as a way to restore the neck's natural curve and reduce forward-head posture, the pattern in which the head sits ahead of the shoulders and the chin juts forward.[4] A neater neck line and a head stacked over the shoulders change how the jaw, neck and profile read, which is the appearance goal people attach to the devices. Users typically pair them with neck and upper-back exercises and with ergonomic changes.

Two different things go by the name. Classic traction pulls the head away from the shoulders, either in a clinic or with an over-door pulley or inflatable collar. Cervical extension traction, promoted by Chiropractic BioPhysics practitioners and by devices such as the Denneroll, instead rests the neck on a contoured roll to encourage the neck's curve, and its published trials measure posture angles directly.[5]

Research on classic traction concerns pain and function rather than posture aesthetics: a 2018 meta-analysis of randomized trials found significant effects of mechanical traction on pain and disability when added to physical therapy for cervical radiculopathy.[2][6] The trials on cervical extension traction do report posture measures, such as a larger craniovertebral angle, and are described below.[5]

paras: Traction is a family of techniques for relieving pressure on the spine or aligning bones, and orthopedic medicine describes skin and skeletal forms; illustrated traction devices appear as early as a Greek device of the 2nd century AD in a Byzantine edition of Galen.[1] Cervical traction applies the same idea to the neck, delivered manually by a therapist or mechanically with a pulley, air or over-door set-up.[2][7]

Wikipedia lists the physiological goals of mechanical traction as separating vertebral bodies, moving the facet joints, widening the openings through which nerves exit and stretching soft tissue, and describes combinations of traction with mobilization, massage, stretching and active exercise as an approach to pain reduction in neck and low back disorders.[1] Reviews of cervical radiculopathy list traction among the conservative options, along with immobilization, anti-inflammatory medication, physical therapy and epidural injections, with at least six weeks of conservative care typical before surgery is considered.[6]

sections.h: Forward head posture and the appearance angle
paras: Forward head posture is described as the head carried ahead of the shoulders with a rounded upper back, so that the earlobes sit forward of the shoulders and the chin projects.[4] Wikipedia describes the look as the ear sitting ahead of the shoulder line, the chin poking forward and the lower neck hinging backward, and says it is now seen in late teenagers as well as older adults.[4] The causes it lists include long hours hunched over laptops, tablets and phones, occupational hunching, and conditions that increase upper-back curvature such as ankylosing spondylitis and Parkinson's disease.[4]

For people working on their looks, the visible consequences are a shorter-looking neck, a less defined jaw-neck angle and a head that sits forward in profile photographs. Posture communities describe correcting this as part of facial presentation as well as comfort. The general treatment advice in reference sources centers on strengthening the deep neck flexors and mid-back, stretching tight neck and upper-trapezius muscles, mobilizing stiff thoracic joints and adjusting ergonomics, and traction devices are discussed as a way to add a decompression or curve-restoring component to that routine.[4]

Wikipedia's article reports adult neck-pain prevalence of 5.9 to 22.2 percent in a 2006 review, notes that forward head posture correlates with neck pain in adults but not in adolescents, and lists physiotherapy, manipulation, massage, yoga, Pilates, the Alexander Technique and ergonomic changes among approaches, pointing to a 2005 randomized trial in which thoracic manipulation reduced neck pain.[4] The article flags parts of its own treatment section as needing independent confirmation.[4]

Home devices range from over-the-door pulley sets to inflatable collars and wedge-shaped neck stretchers; they apply a pulling or arching force that users describe as a stretch for the neck. Clinical traction is delivered by therapists with set parameters, and Wikipedia notes that researchers think inconsistent dosage across studies may explain conflicting trial results.[1][2]

Cervical extension traction is the variant most tied to posture goals. In a 2023 randomized trial, the Denneroll orthotic was used with the patient lying on their back with a contoured roll under the neck at the apex of the neck's curve, extending the cervical segments toward end range without hyperextending the skull; the device was combined with a mirror-image exercise sequence.[5] A machine-learning analysis of 570 patients treated between 2014 and 2020 in a multimodal program that included cervical extension traction modeled changes in cervical lordotic angle, pain and disability from pre-treatment variables including age, body mass index, treatment frequency and compliance.[8]

Alternatives to traction for the same appearance goal include exercise programs. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of ten randomized trials with 550 participants found that therapeutic exercise was associated with an improved craniovertebral angle, less pain and better neck function in people with forward head posture and neck pain.[9]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and posture communities
paras: In posture and looksmaxxing discussions, members describe using such devices alongside neck and upper-back exercises to improve how the head sits over the shoulders and to make the neck and jawline look cleaner in profile. The attraction is that a daily routine may produce a visible change in head position with little equipment. Published trials have measured pain, disability, balance and posture angles, not how the face or neck looks to other people.[2][3][5]

Chiropractic BioPhysics practitioners are the main professional promoters of curve-restoring traction, and several of the trials are authored by the group that develops the technique; the 2023 trial discloses that the devices were supplied by the nonprofit led by its senior author, which is relevant context when weighing the results.[5]
No studies found on cervical traction for the visible appearance of the neck or face.

For posture angle, a 2023 randomized, investigator-blinded trial in 66 adults over 60 with chronic neck pain and a craniovertebral angle below 50 degrees compared Denneroll extension traction plus mirror-image exercises with a standard stretching and strengthening program, in 18 sessions over six weeks.[5] The traction group improved from about 41 to about 55 degrees at six weeks and stayed near 54 at three months, while the exercise group moved from about 43 to about 45 and was about 46 at three months; neck pain was lower in the traction group at three months.[5] The authors listed limitations, including a convenience sample, no untreated control group, short follow-up and the inability to separate the device from the accompanying exercises.[5]

For neck pain, a 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials in cervical radiculopathy reported that mechanical traction had significant effects on pain at short and intermediate follow-up and on disability at intermediate term when added to other physical therapy, with the quality of evidence assessed using GRADE.[2] Wikipedia summarizes a 2018 meta-analysis reporting reduced pain with added traction, a 2020 study favoring mechanical over manual traction, and a 2017 review that rated guideline support as low quality; researchers have suggested inconsistent dosage across studies may explain conflicting results.[1]

A 2009 multicenter randomized trial examined manual therapy, exercise and traction for radiculopathy, noting that evidence for mechanical traction had been limited.[3] A 2025 systematic review and network meta-analysis of manual therapy for cervical radiculopathy pooled eight randomized studies with 632 participants and evaluated neck disability and pain outcomes.[10] A 2021 double-blinded randomized trial of 66 patients compared cervical traction with and without neural mobilization on pain, function and disability.[7] A 1982 physiotherapy paper also reviews neck traction.[11] A 2026 multicenter trial randomized 154 adults with degenerative-disc-related neck pain to rotation-traction manipulation or cervical traction; both groups improved in pain and range of motion.[12] A 2025 randomised trial examined cervical traction's effect on balance parameters in patients with cervical radiculopathy, and a multicentre trial tested Shi-style cervical manipulations for the same condition.[13][14]

Reviews of radiculopathy stress that symptoms must correlate with the underlying pathology and that neck symptoms can have varied causes, including heart-mimicking presentations, so evaluation by a clinician is part of standard care.[6][15]

Published case reports describe rare serious events after traction. A 2026 emergency-medicine case report described a 56-year-old man who developed ptosis, miosis and neck pain after using a home cervical traction device and was found to have an internal carotid artery dissection; the authors recommended asking about traction device use in such presentations.[16] A 2025 case report described bilateral subdural hematomas in a 51-year-old woman after two weeks of cervical traction therapy, with the authors proposing intracranial hypotension as a mechanism.[17] These are single reports and do not give an incidence. Detailed adverse-event data for home traction devices were not found.

lore.intro: Cervical traction comes up in posture and looksmaxxing conversations as a way to restore the neck's curve and bring the head back over the shoulders for a cleaner profile and jawline.[4][5]

claims.claim: Traction restores the neck's natural curve.
Home neck stretchers decompress the spine and relieve pain.
A better neck posture makes the jaw and neck look more defined.
Exercises and ergonomics matter as much as the device.
